bib.title: Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models", Brandon T. Willard and Rémi Louf (Normal Computing), arXiv:2307.09702v4 [cs.CL], preprint, dated 2023-07-14 (arXiv stamp 19 Aug 2023). No venue; the PDF shows none.

COVERAGE: 28558 of 28558 chars read in one pass, including the references and acknowledgments. No appendices or results tables exist. The only results are one timing plot (Section 3.2) and a few anecdotal outputs. Extraction was clean, apart from the Figure 1 and runtime-plot axes, which came out as loose text. I did not run the figure tool.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Masking the logits and sampling at each step makes output follow a regex or CFG, and the paper builds an index over the vocabulary to find the allowed tokens fast.
 - number: none
 - setup: the mask m(s) zeroes the probability of tokens that would violate the constraint (Algorithm 2).
 - quote: "we can compute an un-normalized conditional distribution by applying a boolean mask m : P (V) → {0, 1}N that restricts the support of the original distribution"
 - where: Section 2.2, p.4

2. The common approach costs O(N) per generated token, where N is the vocabulary size. Indexing the FSM states against the vocabulary brings the average cost to O(1).
 - number: O(N) per token against O(1) on average. N is "often on the order of 10^4 or larger", and N = 50,257 for GPT-2 in the comparison.
 - setup: regex-guided generation. The index σ maps FSM states to the vocabulary tokens that are valid in each state. It is built once, before sampling, and stored as a hash map. This is an asymptotic argument, not a measurement.
 - quote: "This approach entails a fixed O(N ) cost for each token generated, where N is the size of the LLM's vocabulary." and "The result is an algorithm that costs O(1) on average."
 - where: Section 1, p.2

3. In the one runtime test, Guidance's runtime grows steeply with the number of generated tokens, while Outlines stays nearly flat.
 - number: the plot runs to about 120 s on the y-axis for 20–100 generated tokens. The text gives no per-point numbers. I read the plot axes only, and the plot's curve values did not extract.
 - setup: GPT-2, CUDA, temperature 0.1, prompt "What is a good Python variable name?", regex [^\W\d]\w*. Guidance was run with caching off and token_healing off. max_tokens was varied, with one timeit loop and one sample per value.
 - quote: "the observed scaling in the maximum number of sampled tokens is striking and is indicative of the growing computational problem implied by the approach."
 - quote: "(i.e. only one sample is collected for each value of max_tokens)"
 - where: Section 3.2, pp.10–12
 - Treat the abstract's "significantly outperforms existing solutions" as resting on this single run against one library.

4. Guidance's cost grows with sequence length because it re-matches the whole sampled string from the start at every step, and it scans the full vocabulary each time.
 - number: N = 50,257
 - quote: "the Guidance library uses partial regular expression matching–applied from the start of the sampled sequence each time–and must iterate over the LLM's vocabulary ( N = 50 , 257) on each step."
 - where: Section 3.2, p.10

5. The method tracks the FSM state between tokens, so it never re-reads the sequence.
 - number: none
 - setup: the vocabulary is pre-processed from every possible start state, because a multi-character token can match any part of the regex.
 - quote: "we consider starting in every viable FSM state, because the strings in the vocabulary could match arbitrary parts of a regular expression, and those parts are implicitly the FSM states."
 - where: Section 3, p.6

6. Extending to CFGs works with LALR(1) parsers and a pushdown-automaton formulation.
 - number: none
 - setup: the index becomes a trie keyed on parser stack values. This section is a conceptual sketch with no experiment.
 - quote: "the index will need to be a trie data structure in order to allow queries against the parser's stack values."
 - where: Section 4.1, p.15

7. Memory cost: an index for a slightly augmented Python grammar is small even without optimisation.
 - number: about 50 MB
 - setup: "naively constructed" indices built from un-reduced DFAs. The paper does not say which vocabulary was used.
 - quote: "even naively constructed indices (i.e. ones containing unused and redundant parser and FSM state configurations) are still only around 50 MB."
 - where: Section 5, p.16

8. Demonstrations with GPT2-medium (355M parameters) show unguided output wandering off-task while regex-guided output is well formed. These are single anecdotes.
 - number: none, apart from the 355M model size.
 - setup: three prompts with max_tokens=30.
   - Yes/no regex: the guided output was "Is 1+1=2? Always". That is valid under the regex but wrong, and the paper does not comment on it.
   - Year regex: r"\s*19[0-9]{2}" gave "1952".
   - IP regex: gave "2.2.6.1" for the Google DNS address.
 - quote: "In this section we use GPT2-medium (355M parameters) to illustrate how regular expression guided generation works in practice."
 - where: Section 3.1, pp.8–10
 - Useful for the note: the constraint guarantees format, not truth.

9. Guaranteed structure is the stated benefit, and the approach is model agnostic.
 - number: none
 - quote: "enables the construction of reliable interfaces by guaranteeing the structure of the generated text."
 - where: Abstract, p.1
 - quote: "guided LLM generation is used to make LLM model output usable under rigid formatting requirements that are either hard or costly to capture through fine-tuning alone"
 - where: Section 1, p.1

10. Tokenization subtlety: a lexer reading the partial string "def f" would wrongly treat "f" as a complete NAME token. The index handles this by allowing every continuation consistent with a partial match.
 - number: none
 - where: Section 4, p.13

LIMITS
- The authors concede a processing-for-memory trade-off: "Naturally, it makes a trade-off between processing and memory".
- Index memory is theoretically |Q|. They claim it is small "for non-pathological combinations of regular expressions and vocabularies" and give no measurements for regexes other than the Python grammar.
- The evidence is thin. There is one benchmark (a single sample per point, one library, GPT-2, one regex), no accuracy or task-quality results, and no comparison with PICARD, Synchromesh or ReLM. The text says ReLM is most similar, but it does not benchmark against it.
- The paper does not measure whether masking harms output quality. It lists this as future work: quantifying the gap between masked and raw logits.
- Masking can force a valid but wrong answer, as the "Always" example shows.
- The CFG and PDA section has no implementation results.
- Speculative future ideas: use during training or fine-tuning, and "lifting" masks into the model architecture.
- Dated: Outlines API shown (outlines.text.generate, generate.regex) is the mid-2023 version. Guidance has changed since, so the comparison is a 2023 snapshot, and the authors flag possible "configuration oversights".

BUILDS ON
- Kuchnik et al. 2023 (ReLM, transducer formulation; the closest regex-case relative).
- Beurer-Kellner et al. 2023 (LMQL, "Prompting is programming").
- Scholak et al. 2021 (PICARD).
- Poesia et al. 2022 (Synchromesh).
- Geng et al. 2023 (grammar-based constrained decoding).
- Wang et al. 2023 (Grammar Prompting).
- Lew et al. 2023 (SMC steering).
- Microsoft Guidance (2023).
- Rickard 2023 (parserLLM, rellm).
- Weng 2021 (controllable text generation).
- Sipser 1996 (FSM and PDA definitions).
- Sennrich et al. 2015 (subword vocabularies).
- Vaswani et al. 2017.

CODE (verbatim)
- Outlines regex generation, p.8–9:
  guided = generate.regex(model, r"\s*([Yy]es|[Nn]o|[Nn]ever|[Aa]lways)", max_tokens=30)(prompt)
- Algorithm 2 (p.5), the core loop: α ← LLM(s, θ); construct mask m(s); α̃ ← m ⊙ α; sample s̃ ~ Categorical(α̃); stop on EOS.
- Algorithm 4 (p.8): for each v in V, for each state-sequence z accepting v, σ(z0) ← σ(z0) ∪ v.
- Example regex for floats, p.6: ([0-9]*)?\.?[0-9]*

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p.6): FSM masking for the regex ([0-9]*)?\.?[0-9]*. It shows the FSM states and which of the vocabulary strings "A", ".", "42", ".2" and "1" are masked after each sample. This is the quickest way to see the mechanism.
- Unnumbered runtime plot (p.12): runtime in seconds against generated tokens (20–100), for Guidance and Outlines. It is the only quantitative result.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Figure 1 and the runtime plot extracted as loose axis text. I did not read the curve values, so claim 3 has no per-point numbers.
- The reference list has duplicate Synchromesh entries (2022a and 2022b), which is a fault in the source.
- The text says "Section 3.2" when it points at the plot, a cross-reference error in the source.
- I did not read the target note, so I made no match against its claims.
